To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the stable state of a thin film of fluid confined between solid walls is determined by a combination of thermodynamic and kinetic factors.
the metastable state of the thin film is the one with the most layers, and that this state is stable only when the walls are aligned.

(1) the stable state of a thin film is the state that has the lowest free energy; (2) the stable state is not necessarily the state with the lowest energy, because free energy includes the entropy; (3) the stable state can be identified by calculating the entropy of each state, and then comparing the free energy; (4) a stable state can become unstable under shear; (5) a metastable state can become stable under shear.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the thermodynamic stability of thin films of simple fluids confined between solid surfaces under conditions of constant temperature, chemical potential and normal load.
the thermodynamics of confined fluids, with a focus on thin films.
understanding the behavior of confined thin films of simple monatomic liquids, and with developing the capability to predict the behavior of more complex fluids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, under conditions of fixed temperature, chemical potential and normal stress, thin films are stable in the absence of shear.
the metastable states observed experimentally are not stable.
a thin film is always metastable when the solid walls are misaligned.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the stability of thin films under shear can be determined by the normal stress or load, the shear, the temperature, and the chemical potential.
a film of monatomic fluid between two solid walls is stable in the epitaxial phase, provided the walls are properly oriented, and that the shear stress is not too large.
the stability of a film is determined by the number of layers, the alignment of the walls, and the shear rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the thermodynamic stability of thin films is not a simple function of the film's thickness, but is a more complicated function of its thickness and of the orientation of its layers with respect to the walls.
, in the presence of shear, metastability is not a rare occurrence.
the thermodynamic stability of thin films is a complex function of temperature and shear rate, and cannot be inferred from measurements of surface forces alone.
